Detector Efficiency from First Principles: a CdTe Slab in Geant4

A CT simulator has to know, for every photon energy, how much of each photon the detector actually records. BasisSimulator describes this with an efficiency curve η(E). The simplest version, Beer-Lambert, says a photon counts if it interacts in the crystal at all: η = 1 − exp(−μ(E)·d). A real detector loses some of what it stops. Just above a K-edge the absorbed photon knocks an electron out of the innermost (K) shell of an atom; the atom refills that shell by emitting an x ray of a fixed, characteristic energy, and that x ray can fly straight back out of the crystal, taking a fixed piece of the energy with it.

Monte Carlo measures this without building the detector: fire photons one at a time, follow every particle they create through the real physics, and add up what stays. This notebook does that with Geant4 (through Geant4.jl) on the simplest detector there is, a single slab of cadmium telluride (CdTe), and checks each step against something known.

  1. The detector and the beam. What is simulated, drawn to scale.

  2. The physics. How strongly CdTe stops x rays, process by process, as Geant4 computes it.

  3. Following photons. Every step of a few dozen photons: where they stop, where the characteristic x rays go.

  4. Check 1: the Monte Carlo reproduces Beer-Lambert. The fraction of photons that interact must equal 1 − exp(−μd) with Geant4's own μ, to within counting noise.

  5. Where the energy goes. The energy budget per photon (it must add up exactly) and the spectrum of energy left in the crystal, with its escape peaks.

  6. The efficiency curves. What the detector keeps, against what Beer-Lambert predicts, across the CT energy range.

How the Notebook Works

Every number in the notebook comes from Geant4. NIST XCOM (through XrayAttenuation.jl, the attenuation data BasisSimulator uses) appears only as a comparison, so the size of the difference between the two standard data sets is visible wherever it matters. The figure below is the whole experiment: what happens to the photons, what Geant4 follows, and what it records.

# One colour per kind of particle, used by every figure
PALETTE = (
    photon = Mke.RGBf(0.13, 0.36, 0.66),  # the incident photon
    xray = Mke.RGBf(0.9, 0.45, 0.05),  # characteristic (fluorescence) x rays
    electron = Mke.RGBf(0.7, 0.12, 0.17),  # electrons set free in the crystal
    kept = Mke.RGBf(0.27, 0.55, 0.34),  # energy that stays in the crystal
    slab = Mke.RGBAf(0.45, 0.52, 0.62, 0.3),
    slab_edge = Mke.RGBf(0.3, 0.36, 0.44),
    ink = Mke.RGBf(0.13, 0.13, 0.16),
    muted = Mke.RGBf(0.42, 0.42, 0.46),
)
Attributes with 6 entries: Axis => Attributes() Axis3 => Attributes() figure_padding => (12, 24, 12, 12) fontsize => 18 Legend => Attributes() Lines => Attributes()
# Large, uncluttered type for every figure
THEME = Mke.Theme(
    fontsize = 18,
    figure_padding = (12, 24, 12, 12),
    Axis = (
        titlesize = 21,
        titlealign = :left,
        titlegap = 14,
        xlabelsize = 19,
        ylabelsize = 19,
        xticklabelsize = 16,
        yticklabelsize = 16,
        xgridcolor = (:black, 0.07),
        ygridcolor = (:black, 0.07),
        topspinevisible = false,
        rightspinevisible = false,
        xlabelpadding = 8,
        ylabelpadding = 12,
    ),
    Axis3 = (
        titlesize = 21,
        titlealign = :left,
        xlabelsize = 18,
        ylabelsize = 18,
        zlabelsize = 18,
        xticklabelsize = 15,
        yticklabelsize = 15,
        zticklabelsize = 15,
    ),
    Legend = (
        labelsize = 17,
        framevisible = false,
        patchsize = (30, 14),
        rowgap = 8,
    ),
    Lines = (
        linewidth = 2.5,
    ),
)
note! (generic function with 1 method)
"""
An in-figure annotation on a translucent rounded background, so it never fights the data.
"""
function note!(
        ax, x, y, text;
        align = (:left, :center),
        color = PALETTE.ink,
        fontsize = 16,
        offset = (0, 0),
        alpha = 0.85,
    )
    return Mke.textlabel!(
        ax, Mke.Point2f(x, y);
        text,
        text_align = align,
        text_color = color,
        fontsize,
        offset,
        background_color = (:white, alpha),
        strokewidth = 0,
        padding = (7, 7, 4, 4),
        cornerradius = 5,
    )
end

Drawing the Detector

The illustrations are drawn from the same numbers the simulation uses, with a small kit: blocks in 3-D seen from any direction (shaded by one light, drawn back to front), photons as waves, and labels on translucent backgrounds. Their colours are the plots' colours: blue for the incoming photon, orange for characteristic x rays, dark red for electrons, green for the energy that stays.

# The crystal and the beam, as the illustrations draw them: the same colours as the plots
MATERIALS = (
    cdte = Mke.RGBf(0.8, 0.83, 0.89),  # the CdTe crystal
    beam = PALETTE.photon,  # the incoming photons
    star = Mke.RGBf(0.98, 0.95, 0.6),  # where a photon is absorbed

Block
begin
    """A block in 3-D (axis-aligned, `lo` to `hi` in mm), and how to draw it."""
    Base.@kwdef struct Block
        lo::NTuple{3, Float64}
        hi::NTuple{3, Float64}
        color::Mke.RGBf
        alpha::Float64 = 1.0
        stroke::Float64 = 0.6
    end

    Block(lo, hi, color; kw...) = Block(; lo = Float64.(Tuple(lo)), hi = Float64.(Tuple(hi)), color, kw...)
end
camera (generic function with 1 method)
"""
An orthographic camera: seen from `azimuth` (degrees, about the vertical axis z) and `elevation`
(degrees above the horizontal). Returns the screen's right and up and the direction toward the viewer.
"""
function camera(azimuth, elevation)
    θ, φ = deg2rad(azimuth), deg2rad(elevation)
    toward = (cos(φ) * cos(θ), cos(φ) * sin(θ), sin(φ))
    right = (-sin(θ), cos(θ), 0.0)
    up = (
        toward[2] * right[3] - toward[3] * right[2],
        toward[3] * right[1] - toward[1] * right[3],
        toward[1] * right[2] - toward[2] * right[1],
    )
    return (; right, up, toward)
end
dot3 (generic function with 1 method)
dot3(a, b) = a[1] * b[1] + a[2] * b[2] + a[3] * b[3]
project (generic function with 1 method)
"""Where a point in 3-D lands on the drawing."""
project(cam, p) = Mke.Point2f(dot3(p, cam.right), dot3(p, cam.up))
faces (generic function with 1 method)
"""The six faces of a block: outward normal and corners."""
function faces(b::Block)
    (x0, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z1) = b.lo, b.hi
    return (
        ((0, 0, 1), ((x0, y0, z1), (x1, y0, z1), (x1, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z1))),
        ((0, 0, -1), ((x0, y0, z0), (x0, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y0, z0))),
        ((1, 0, 0), ((x1, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z0), (x1, y1, z1), (x1, y0, z1))),
        ((-1, 0, 0), ((x0, y0, z0), (x0, y0, z1), (x0, y1, z1), (x0, y1, z0))),
        ((0, 1, 0), ((x0, y1, z0), (x0, y1, z1), (x1, y1, z1), (x1, y1, z0))),
        ((0, -1, 0), ((x0, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z0), (x1, y0, z1), (x0, y0, z1))),
    )
end
shade (generic function with 1 method)
"""Shade a face by one light from the upper left, front, as illustrators do."""
function shade(color, normal, cam; light = (-0.35, -0.45, 0.82))
    n = sqrt(dot3(light, light))
    lambert = max(0.0, dot3(normal, light) / n)
    k = 0.62 + 0.42 * lambert
    return Mke.RGBf(min(1, color.r * k), min(1, color.g * k), min(1, color.b * k))
end
draw_blocks! (generic function with 1 method)
"""
Draw `blocks` back to front (the painter's way), each with its visible faces shaded, and any
`extras` (functions drawing lines or arrows, with their depth) in their place among them.
Blocks should be of similar size (split long walls into pieces) for the order to be right.
"""
function draw_blocks!(ax, cam, blocks; extras = [], edge = Mke.RGBf(0.1, 0.12, 0.16), edge_alpha = 0.35)
    items = Any[(dot3(map(+, b.lo, b.hi) ./ 2, cam.toward), b) for b in blocks]
    append!(items, extras)
    sort!(items; by = first)
    polygons = Vector{Mke.Point2f}[]
    colors = Mke.RGBAf[]
    strokes = Mke.RGBAf[]
    function flush!()
        isempty(polygons) && return
        Mke.poly!(
            ax,
            copy(polygons);
            color = copy(colors),
            strokecolor = copy(strokes),
            strokewidth = 0.7,
        )
        empty!(polygons)
        empty!(colors)
        return empty!(strokes)
    end
    for (_, item) in items
        if item isa Block
            for (normal, corners) in faces(item)
                dot3(normal, cam.toward) > 1.0e-9 || continue
                push!(polygons, [project(cam, c) for c in corners])
                c = shade(item.color, normal, cam)
                push!(colors, Mke.RGBAf(c.r, c.g, c.b, item.alpha))
                # a seam between tiles of one layer is drawn in the face's own colour
                push!(
                    strokes,
                    item.stroke > 0 ? Mke.RGBAf(edge.r, edge.g, edge.b, edge_alpha * item.alpha) :
                        Mke.RGBAf(c.r, c.g, c.b, item.alpha),
                )
            end
        else
            flush!()
            item(ax)
        end
    end
    flush!()
    return ax
end
canvas (generic function with 1 method)
"""A blank canvas for an illustration: equal scales, no axes."""
function canvas(position; background = :white, title = "", kw...)
    ax = Mke.Axis(
        position;
        aspect = Mke.DataAspect(),
        backgroundcolor = background,
        title,
        kw...,
    )
    Mke.hidedecorations!(ax)
    Mke.hidespines!(ax)
    return ax
end
photon! (generic function with 1 method)
"""
A photon drawn as a wave from `a` to `b` (2-D), with `cycles` oscillations (more for a higher
energy) and an arrowhead at `b`.
"""
function photon!(ax, a, b; color = MATERIALS.beam, cycles = 6, amplitude = 0.06, linewidth = 3, head = 14)
    a, b = Mke.Point2f(a), Mke.Point2f(b)
    d = b - a
    L = sqrt(d[1]^2 + d[2]^2)
    t = d / L
    n = Mke.Point2f(-t[2], t[1])
    s = range(0, 1; length = 240)
    ramp(u) = min(1, 8u, 8(1 - u))  # the wave starts and ends on the line
    points = Mke.Point2f[a + u * d + amplitude * L * ramp(u) * sin(2π * cycles * u) * n for u in s]
    Mke.lines!(ax, points[1:(end - 6)]; color, linewidth)
    Mke.scatter!(
        ax,
        [b];
        marker = :utriangle,
        markersize = head,
        rotation = atan(t[2], t[1]) - π / 2,
        color,
    )
    return nothing
end
arrow! (generic function with 1 method)
"""A straight arrow from `a` to `b` (2-D)."""
function arrow!(ax, a, b; color = MATERIALS.beam, linewidth = 3, head = 14, linestyle = :solid)
    a, b = Mke.Point2f(a), Mke.Point2f(b)
    t = (b - a) / sqrt(sum(abs2, b - a))
    Mke.lines!(ax, Mke.Point2f[a, b - 0.5 * head / 100 * t]; color, linewidth, linestyle)
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [b]; marker = :utriangle, markersize = head, rotation = atan(t[2], t[1]) - π / 2, color)
    return nothing
end
rect! (generic function with 1 method)
"""A rectangle (2-D) from its lower-left corner, width and height."""
rect!(ax, x, y, w, h, color; kw...) = Mke.poly!(ax, Mke.Rect2f(x, y, w, h); color, kw...)
callout! (generic function with 1 method)
"""
A label with a leader line: a dot at `anchor`, a line to `at`, and the text there, on a
translucent rounded background.
"""
function callout!(
        ax,
        anchor,
        at,
        text;
        color = Mke.RGBf(0.13, 0.13, 0.16),
        align = (:left, :center),
        fontsize = 17,
        background = (:white, 0.9),
        line = (Mke.RGBf(0.3, 0.3, 0.35), 0.8),
        font = :regular,
    )
    Mke.lines!(ax, Mke.Point2f[anchor, at]; color = line, linewidth = 1.3)
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [anchor]; color = line, markersize = 7)
    return Mke.textlabel!(
        ax,
        at;
        text,
        text_align = align,
        text_color = color,
        fontsize,
        font,
        background_color = background,
        strokewidth = 0,
        padding = (8, 8, 5, 5),
        cornerradius = 6,
    )
end
tag! (generic function with 1 method)
"""A small rounded tag ("In Geant4" / "Not Simulated")."""
function tag!(ax, at, text, color; align = (:left, :center), fontsize = 14, offset = (0, 0))
    return Mke.textlabel!(
        ax,
        at;
        text,
        text_align = align,
        text_color = :white,
        font = :bold,
        fontsize,
        offset,
        background_color = color,
        strokewidth = 0,
        padding = (8, 8, 3, 3),
        cornerradius = 9,
    )
end

TAGS = (geant4 = Mke.RGBf(0.2, 0.55, 0.32), not_simulated = Mke.RGBf(0.52, 0.52, 0.57))
atom! (generic function with 1 method)
"""A Gd atom: nucleus and two shells, at `c` with outer radius `r`."""
function atom!(ax, c, r; color = Mke.RGBf(0.45, 0.47, 0.55))
    θ = range(0, 2π; length = 100)
    for (k, rr) in enumerate((0.55r, r))
        Mke.lines!(ax, c[1] .+ rr .* cos.(θ), c[2] .+ rr .* sin.(θ); color = (color, 0.55), linewidth = 1.5)
    end
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [Mke.Point2f(c)]; color, markersize = 18)
    return nothing
end

1. The Detector and the Beam

The detector is one block of cadmium telluride, the crystal photon-counting CT scanners use, 1 mm deep along the beam and 50 mm square across it, in vacuum. A narrow ("pencil") beam of photons, all of the same energy, hits the centre of its front face head on.

Which beam, and why. A pencil beam is enough here, and exact: the slab is uniform and 50 mm wide, and nothing travels more than a few millimetres in CdTe, so a photon landing anywhere on the face sees the same crystal around it. A pencil beam into the centre gives what a uniform beam over the whole face would, for the slab as one detector. Pixels, their edges and their neighbours are not part of this notebook; notebook 03 builds them, and there the beam matters.

The coordinates used by every figure and every number below: z runs along the beam and photons travel toward +z; the front (entrance) face is at z = 0 and the back face at z = d; x and y run across the face. The 50 mm face is far wider than anything travels in CdTe, so nothing leaks out of the sides and the only ways out are back through the front face or on through the back face.

2. The Physics

Three things can happen to an x-ray photon in CdTe at CT energies. Their strengths, written as attenuation coefficients μ (the chance of the interaction per millimetre travelled), add up to the total μ that Beer-Lambert uses:

  • Photoelectric absorption: the photon is absorbed. An electron of an atom takes all its energy and is set free; the atom then refills the empty shell by emitting electrons (which stop within micrometres) or a characteristic x ray (which can travel a millimetre). This dominates in CdTe at every CT energy, and it jumps up at each K-edge, the energy above which the photon can free an electron from the innermost (K) shell.

  • Compton scattering: the photon bounces off an electron and loses part of its energy, then carries on in a new direction and can leave the crystal.

  • Rayleigh scattering: the photon bounces off a whole atom and keeps its energy.

The solid curves are Geant4's own coefficients, from the models the simulation samples. The dashed curves are NIST XCOM, for comparison; the lower panel shows how far apart the two data sets are. They agree to about 1 % for absorption and Compton scattering. Rayleigh scattering differs by up to about 25 %: Geant4's Livermore model includes the drop in coherent scattering just below and at each K-edge (the atom's K electrons stop scattering in step with the photon), which XCOM's tables leave out. Rayleigh scattering is a small part of the total, so the total moves by less than 2 %, and only right at the edges.

3. Following Photons

record_tracks fires a few dozen photons and keeps every step of every particle they set moving. Panel (a) is the side view of figure 1(b): the beam comes in from the left and the grey band is the crystal. Panel (b) magnifies one absorption about a hundred times.

What to look for: almost every photon is absorbed (red dot) in the first few hundred micrometres, because μ is large. Many absorptions send out a characteristic x ray (orange) in a random direction, which travels up to a millimetre before it is absorbed in turn. The ones that start near the front face and head backward get out of the crystal, and their energy is lost to the detector: this is K-escape. The electron the photon frees (dark red, panel b) stops within about a micrometre, so its energy stays where it was made.

4. Check 1: the Monte Carlo Reproduces Beer-Lambert

Before any detector physics is trusted, the simplest number must come out right. The fraction of photons that interact at all (absorbed or scattered) is exactly 1 − exp(−μd). The Monte Carlo gets it by firing photons and counting; Beer-Lambert gets it from a formula. With Geant4's own μ in the formula, the two must agree to within counting noise at every energy. If the geometry, the density, the composition or the beam were wrong, they would not.

The sweep fires 100 000 photons at every whole keV from 10 to 140 keV, BasisSimulator's energy grid, spread over the eight worker processes started in the setup. Every photon's record is kept, so sections 5 and 6 reuse these runs.

128 of the 131 energies, 98 %, agree with Geant4's Beer-Lambert to within twice the counting noise (about 95 % would by pure chance), and the largest disagreement is 2.4 × the noise. Against XCOM's Beer-Lambert the largest difference is 0.11 percentage points: the size of the disagreement between the two standard cross-section data sets.

5. Where the Energy Goes

Energy is conserved photon by photon: everything the incoming photon brought is either left in the crystal or carried out by something that escaped. The budget below adds those up over all photons at each energy. The top of the stack must be exactly 1.

Largest departure of the total from 1 over all energies: 2.5e-9. No energy is created or lost by the simulation's bookkeeping.

The spectrum of energy left in the crystal

At one photon energy, the histogram of the energy each photon left behind shows every way of losing energy as its own feature. The top panel is what escaped as characteristic x rays: sharp lines, the fingerprints of Cd and Te. The bottom panel is what stayed: a full-energy peak at the photon energy, and for every line above an escape peak at the photon energy minus that line, made by the photons whose x ray got out. The numbers match each escaped line to its escape peak. (Kα and Kβ are the two strongest characteristic lines of each element; Kβ is the rarer, slightly more energetic one.)

6. The Efficiency Curves

Three numbers summarise a detector at each energy:

  • Quantum efficiency: the fraction of photons that leave any energy in the crystal. A photon-counting detector with a low threshold counts these.

  • Energy-absorption efficiency: the average energy a photon leaves, as a fraction of its energy. An energy-integrating (scintillator) detector's signal is proportional to it; it is the quantity in the Monte Carlo tables BasisSimulator v0.15.1 used, and in the Geant4 tables of notebooks 04–08 that replace them.

  • Swank factor: how alike the energies left by the detected photons are. It is 1 when every detected photon leaves the same energy, and it falls as they spread out (escape peaks, scatter). The zero-frequency DQE of an energy-integrating detector is the quantum efficiency times the Swank factor.

Beer-Lambert counts every interaction, so it sits slightly above the quantum efficiency: a photon that only bounces out of the crystal (Rayleigh) interacted but left nothing. It cannot predict the energy-absorption efficiency at all: just above each K-edge absorption gets more likely, yet the energy kept drops, because every characteristic x ray that escapes takes its energy with it.
